items.content_html:
Diesel particulate filter (DPF) systems operate in demanding thermal and mechanical environments, making the housing around the filter more than a simple sheet-metal enclosure. A properly fabricated DPF housing must accommodate the filter assembly, exhaust inlet and outlet connections, mounting interfaces, sensor provisions, thermal conditions, vibration, service access, and the dimensional requirements of the equipment into which it is installed. For OEM equipment, industrial machinery, generators, construction equipment, and retrofit applications, custom fabrication can be necessary when a standard housing does not match the available space or connection geometry.

dpf housing fabrication combines metal fabrication, dimensional control, welding, forming, machining, and application-specific engineering considerations. Material selection may involve stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, or specialized high-temperature materials depending on the operating environment and location of each component. The fabrication process can also incorporate mounting brackets, reinforcement structures, flanges, clamps, inspection openings, heat shields, and sensor ports.

For engineers, contractors, equipment manufacturers, and procurement teams, the critical question is not simply whether a fabricator can produce a metal enclosure. The important consideration is whether the fabricated assembly can be developed around the actual operating conditions, equipment interfaces, manufacturing tolerances, and project requirements.

The Sigma Source approaches custom metal fabrication from this engineering perspective. Its capabilities in CAD modeling, laser and plasma cutting, forming, machining, welding, and custom metal fabrication can support projects requiring application-specific fabricated assemblies. The appropriate fabrication scope, however, should always be established from the equipment documentation, material requirements, operating conditions, and applicable regulatory or engineering requirements rather than from a generic housing design.

What Is DPF Housing Fabrication?

DPF housing fabrication is the process of manufacturing the structural enclosure or canister that packages and supports a diesel particulate filter within a diesel exhaust or aftertreatment system. The housing provides the physical structure around the filter assembly while creating defined interfaces for exhaust flow, mounting, service, and instrumentation.

A DPF housing should be distinguished from the DPF filter itself. The filter substrate is the component responsible for trapping particulate matter from diesel exhaust. The housing provides the mechanical enclosure and interfaces required to integrate that filter into the broader exhaust system. Depending on the application, the fabricated assembly may connect with exhaust piping, flanges, clamps, sensor ports, mounting brackets, heat shields, and supporting structures.

Custom DPF housing fabrication becomes particularly useful when equipment-specific constraints prevent the use of an off-the-shelf enclosure. An industrial diesel engine may have limited installation space, unusual exhaust routing, unique mounting locations, or dimensional requirements dictated by existing machinery. A retrofit project may also require a replacement housing that matches existing piping while accommodating new mounting provisions.

The housing geometry must therefore be considered as part of the complete installation rather than as an isolated component. Inlet and outlet locations, surrounding clearances, support points, service access, sensor locations, and connection interfaces all influence the final fabrication.

For a technical buyer, this distinction matters because a fabricator may be capable of producing the metal enclosure without being responsible for the emissions performance or certification of the complete aftertreatment system. The fabrication scope and emissions-system responsibilities should be clearly defined before production begins.

Key Design Considerations for a Custom DPF Housing

A custom DPF housing should be developed from actual operating and installation requirements. One of the first considerations is temperature. Diesel exhaust systems can experience substantial thermal cycling, so the housing material, joints, gaskets, insulation, coatings, and nearby components must be appropriate for the expected environment. Temperature information should be established from equipment documentation or the responsible engineering team rather than assumed from the housing's appearance or general application.

Thermal expansion is another important consideration. Repeated heating and cooling can cause dimensional changes in metal components. If a housing is rigidly connected to surrounding components without accounting for movement, thermal cycling can contribute to stress at joints, mounting points, or connected exhaust piping. The appropriate design response depends on the system configuration and should be established as part of the project engineering.

Exhaust connection geometry is equally important. Inlet and outlet positions, pipe diameters, flange dimensions, V-band interfaces, transitions, and available installation space all affect fabrication. Small dimensional errors can create installation problems when the housing must connect to existing exhaust components.

Mechanical loading should also be considered. Diesel equipment produces vibration, and mobile machinery can introduce additional movement and shock. The housing, brackets, hangers, and supporting structure must therefore be coordinated with the equipment's mounting arrangement.

These factors demonstrate why custom DPF housing fabrication should begin with dimensional and application information rather than simply selecting a material and cutting a shell. The housing needs to function as part of a complete mechanical assembly.

Materials Used in DPF Housing Fabrication

Material selection for a DPF housing depends on temperature, corrosion exposure, mechanical loading, weight, fabrication requirements, and the location of the component within the exhaust assembly. There is no universal material that is appropriate for every DPF application.

Stainless steel is frequently considered for exhaust-related fabrication because certain stainless grades provide useful combinations of corrosion resistance, strength, fabricability, and elevated-temperature performance. Grades such as 304 and 316 may be considered where their properties align with the actual application. However, grade selection should not be made solely because stainless steel is generally associated with exhaust systems. Temperature, chemical exposure, environmental conditions, fabrication requirements, and project specifications should guide the decision.

Carbon steel can also be appropriate for selected housing structures and support components where its mechanical and fabrication characteristics satisfy the application. Its use may be practical when temperature, corrosion protection, structural requirements, and cost considerations are compatible with the intended location.

Aluminum requires more careful application-specific evaluation because its temperature capability differs significantly from many stainless and carbon steel options. It may be useful for certain surrounding components or lower-temperature applications, but its suitability must be evaluated against actual thermal conditions.

Other high-temperature alloys or specialized materials may be required in particularly demanding environments. Material selection should consider not only the housing shell but also flanges, brackets, reinforcement rings, fasteners, gaskets, sensor interfaces, and other connected components.

Surface treatments also require context. Galvanizing, powder coating, or other finishes may be appropriate for selected external components, but a coating must be compatible with the actual service temperature and exposure. A finish that works well on general fabricated steel cannot automatically be assumed suitable for a high-temperature exhaust surface.

DPF Housing Fabrication Processes

A reliable fabrication workflow begins with engineering documentation and dimensional development. Depending on the project, this may involve existing drawings, measurements, CAD files, equipment models, or a new three-dimensional CAD model. Critical interfaces should be identified before fabrication so that mounting points, exhaust connections, service openings, and other features can be located accurately.

Laser cutting and plasma cutting can be used for appropriately specified sheet and plate components. Forming, rolling, and bending processes can then produce the required housing geometry. The choice of process depends on material, thickness, geometry, tolerances, production quantity, and the required finished configuration.

Welding is a central part of many DPF housing assemblies. TIG and MIG processes may be appropriate for different materials and joint configurations. Joint preparation, fixture design, weld sequence, and heat input can influence distortion and dimensional accuracy. For assemblies containing multiple welded components, fabrication planning becomes particularly important because localized heating can change the geometry of the finished structure.

CNC machining may be incorporated when the housing requires accurately machined interfaces, mounting surfaces, holes, or other precision features. Machining can be performed as part of an integrated fabrication workflow when the project requires tighter control than cutting and forming alone can provide.

Final assembly and inspection should verify the critical dimensions and interfaces identified in the project documentation. Depending on the scope, this can include checking mounting-hole locations, flange geometry, overall dimensions, sensor-port positions, and other interfaces that directly affect installation.

This integrated approach allows diesel particulate filter housing fabrication to be treated as an engineered metal assembly rather than a generic enclosure.

DPF Housing Components and Mounting Features

A custom DPF housing can incorporate numerous components beyond the primary enclosure. Mounting brackets and support plates are often important because the housing must be supported within the equipment without creating unnecessary loads on exhaust piping or other components. Reinforcement structures may also be required around mounting locations or connection points depending on the mechanical configuration.

Flanges, clamps, and exhaust connections define how the housing interfaces with upstream and downstream components. V-band connections, flanged joints, gaskets, and other connection methods should be specified according to the equipment design and applicable requirements. Dimensional accuracy at these interfaces is particularly important because an otherwise well-fabricated housing can become difficult to install if its connection geometry does not match the surrounding exhaust system.

Instrumentation can introduce additional fabrication requirements. Temperature sensor ports, differential-pressure connections, and other sensor provisions may need to be positioned according to the requirements of the particular aftertreatment system. Inspection and service openings can also be incorporated where maintenance procedures require access.

Thermal protection may include heat shields or insulation around portions of the assembly. The objective is not simply to reduce the apparent temperature of the housing but to manage heat exposure to adjacent equipment, wiring, structural components, and personnel-access areas where applicable.

In mobile and industrial equipment, mounting design should also account for vibration and movement. Brackets, hangers, and supports should be coordinated with the equipment's existing structure and operating conditions. Where a vibration-isolation component is genuinely required, it should be selected based on the relevant mechanical and environmental requirements rather than added as a generic feature.

The result is a fabricated assembly that addresses the complete installation interface instead of treating the DPF canister as an independent metal shell.

Custom DPF Housing Fabrication for Industrial and Heavy-Duty Equipment

Industrial and heavy-duty equipment often creates fabrication conditions that differ substantially from standard automotive applications. Diesel generators, construction equipment, agricultural machinery, mining equipment, marine engines, and other industrial platforms can have highly specific packaging and exhaust requirements.

Diesel generators may require custom exhaust packaging around an engine enclosure, skid, or equipment support structure. Available space can be restricted by other generator components, while the exhaust route may require specific bends, connection points, and support locations. A fabricated housing may therefore need to coordinate with the generator's physical arrangement and the surrounding exhaust system.

Construction and off-road equipment introduces additional considerations because the machinery may experience vibration, movement, dust, moisture, impact exposure, and changing operating conditions. The housing and its support components should be designed around the actual equipment environment rather than treated as a stationary industrial assembly.

Marine and industrial engines can present their own requirements. Marine environments may increase corrosion concerns, while industrial installations may impose tight spatial restrictions or require integration with existing machinery. Equipment used in manufacturing facilities can also have specific maintenance-access requirements that influence housing geometry.

For each application, the fabrication scope should be tied to the actual engine, equipment configuration, exhaust system, and installation environment. A heavy-duty DPF housing is not simply a larger version of a smaller enclosure. Its material selection, mounting structure, fabrication process, and inspection requirements should reflect the loads and conditions associated with the equipment.

This application-specific approach is especially important for custom and replacement work, where the housing must fit an existing mechanical environment rather than a standardized equipment platform.

DPF Housing Fabrication for OEM and Retrofit Applications

OEM and retrofit projects can require very different fabrication workflows. In new equipment integration, the housing can be developed around the equipment architecture before production begins. CAD models can establish the available installation envelope, connection geometry, mounting interfaces, and relationships with surrounding components. This can make it easier to identify interference problems before fabrication.

Production work also places greater emphasis on repeatability. Once a prototype or initial assembly has been validated, subsequent housings need to maintain the specified dimensions and interfaces. Consistent fixtures, fabrication sequences, inspection procedures, and documentation can help support repeatable production.

Retrofit and replacement applications can be more challenging because the existing equipment may already be installed. Measurements must account for real-world conditions, existing exhaust routing, mounting points, available clearances, and components that cannot easily be relocated. A replacement housing may need to reproduce certain interfaces while introducing new features to address changes in the equipment.

For a retrofit, the available information should include photographs, field measurements, existing drawings where available, equipment identification, DPF dimensions, inlet and outlet geometry, and mounting details. When the original manufacturer housing is unavailable, these details become especially important for developing a replacement assembly.

The fabrication partner should also understand the distinction between modifying physical hardware and modifying a regulated emissions system. A custom housing can be fabricated to specified dimensions and interfaces, but the implications for the complete emissions-control system should be reviewed by the responsible equipment manufacturer, emissions specialist, or engineer when applicable.

For both OEM and retrofit work, prototype validation can reduce the risk of discovering dimensional or installation problems only after a production quantity has been manufactured.

Quality Control Considerations for Fabricated DPF Housings

Quality control for DPF housing fabrication should focus on the characteristics that affect fit, function, durability, and integration. Dimensional accuracy is one of the first considerations. Critical dimensions may include overall housing size, inlet and outlet locations, flange geometry, mounting-hole patterns, bracket positions, sensor ports, and service openings.

Weld quality is also important. The appropriate welding process depends on the selected material and joint configuration. Joint preparation, fit-up, heat input, welding sequence, and distortion control can all affect the final assembly. A housing that is dimensionally accurate before welding can shift during fabrication if the assembly sequence is not properly controlled.

Inspection should therefore be tied to project requirements rather than limited to a visual check of the completed housing. Critical interfaces should be verified against drawings, CAD data, or approved dimensional information. Where the project requires specific welding inspection or documentation, those requirements should be established before fabrication.

Material identification and traceability can also matter for engineered industrial assemblies. Depending on the project, documentation may include material certifications, drawings, inspection records, welding documentation, or other quality records.

The procurement team should establish these expectations early. If dimensional inspection or material documentation is needed at delivery, it is better to define the requirements during quotation and fabrication planning rather than after the assembly has been completed.

A technically capable DPF housing manufacturer should therefore be evaluated not only on its ability to cut and weld metal but also on its ability to control the complete fabrication process and document the characteristics that matter to the end application.

DPF Housing Fabrication and Applicable U.S. Requirements

Applicable requirements for a DPF housing depend on its function, equipment, installation, jurisdiction, and relationship to the complete emissions-control system. This distinction is important because not every fabricated exhaust component is automatically governed by the same standards or certification framework.

EPA and California Air Resources Board requirements may become relevant when a fabricated component forms part of a regulated emissions-control system. The fabricator should not represent the production of a metal housing alone as certification of the emissions performance of the complete DPF or aftertreatment system. The applicable requirements should be established from the engine, equipment, emissions configuration, and jurisdiction.

Building and structural codes can also enter the project when the housing or its support structure is installed as part of a larger facility or engineered installation. IBC and CBC requirements may be relevant to building-related supporting structures depending on the scope. ASCE 7 may become relevant where structural or seismic design of supporting elements falls within the project requirements.

Similarly, AWS, ASTM, SAE, or ASME standards may apply to specific materials, welding procedures, components, or fabrication requirements. Their relevance should be determined by the project specification and responsible engineering discipline rather than simply adding standards to a product description.

For healthcare and other regulated facilities, additional project requirements may apply to the supporting structure, equipment installation, or facility-specific engineering documentation. OSHPD/HCAI requirements should likewise be addressed where applicable to the facility and scope rather than presented as universal DPF-housing requirements.

The practical approach is to identify applicable requirements during project definition, establish which party is responsible for compliance, and ensure the fabricated assembly is produced according to the approved engineering and procurement documentation.

How to Specify a Custom DPF Housing Fabrication Project

A well-defined fabrication package gives the fabricator enough information to understand both the physical assembly and the conditions under which it will operate. The starting point should include the DPF dimensions and the engine or equipment application. Inlet and outlet dimensions, connection types, mounting locations, and the available installation envelope are also essential.

Operating temperature information should be provided whenever available because it directly affects material and component selection. Environmental exposure should also be identified, particularly where the equipment will operate outdoors, in corrosive environments, around water, or in industrial facilities.

The project package should identify material requirements, desired finish, sensor locations, flange or clamp specifications, exhaust routing, production quantity, and applicable project standards. Existing CAD drawings, three-dimensional models, manufacturer drawings, or accurate field measurements can substantially improve the fabrication process.

Information to Provide the Fabricator

A useful specification package can include:

  • DPF dimensions and configuration

  • Engine model and equipment application

  • Exhaust inlet and outlet dimensions

  • Operating temperature information

  • Material requirements

  • Mounting locations

  • Available installation envelope

  • Sensor and instrumentation locations

  • Flange or clamp specifications

  • Exhaust routing

  • Environmental exposure

  • Required finish

  • Production quantity

  • CAD drawings or reference models

  • Applicable project standards

The transition from prototype to production deserves particular attention. A prototype may reveal installation conflicts, bracket changes, access requirements, or dimensional adjustments that should be incorporated before production quantities are released. Once the design is established, repeatable fabrication and inspection requirements can help maintain consistency across subsequent assemblies.

This process is especially valuable for OEM and industrial procurement teams because it turns an informal fabrication request into a defined engineering and manufacturing scope.

Why Custom Metal Fabrication Capabilities Matter for DPF Housings

DPF housing fabrication often requires several manufacturing processes within one assembly. A fabricator that can coordinate CAD development, cutting, forming, machining, welding, assembly, and inspection can reduce the need to divide a complex project among multiple suppliers.

CAD modeling is useful for establishing the housing geometry and checking interfaces before manufacturing. Laser and plasma cutting can produce accurately defined components from appropriate materials and thicknesses, while forming processes create cylindrical, bent, or otherwise shaped sections. CNC machining can provide precision features where required.

Welding then brings the individual components together. For stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, or other specified materials, the welding process should be selected according to the material and joint requirements. Fixtures and controlled assembly sequences can help maintain dimensional accuracy.

Surface finishing should also be selected according to service conditions. A general-purpose finish should not be treated as automatically suitable for a component exposed to elevated temperatures or aggressive environments.

The Sigma Source's broader custom metal fabrication capabilities encompass stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, sheet metal, structural steel, cutting, forming, machining, welding, and related processes. These capabilities provide a foundation for producing application-specific fabricated components when the project requirements are clearly defined.

The same principle applies to engineering support. BIM and 3D CAD capabilities can help translate equipment dimensions and connection requirements into a manufacturable model, while project coordination can help align fabrication with the broader construction or equipment-integration schedule. The objective is not to add unrelated engineering services to a DPF project, but to use the capabilities that are genuinely relevant to the fabrication scope.

Selecting a DPF Housing Fabrication Partner

Selecting a fabrication partner should involve more than comparing unit prices. Engineers, OEMs, contractors, and procurement teams should evaluate whether the supplier has the material capabilities, manufacturing processes, engineering support, and quality controls required by the project.

Relevant metal fabrication experience is a starting point, particularly when the housing requires multiple processes. Material capabilities should match the proposed design, while welding capabilities should align with the specified metals and joint configurations. CAD support can be valuable when the project requires custom geometry or when existing equipment must be modeled before fabrication.

Prototype capability is another consideration. A supplier that can support an initial prototype and then transition the validated design into repeatable production can simplify projects involving custom equipment.

Dimensional quality control and documentation should be discussed before fabrication. If the project requires inspection records, material documentation, or defined acceptance criteria, those requirements should be included in the procurement package.

Thermal and vibration considerations are also relevant. The supplier should understand that the housing operates within an equipment system and that mounting, exhaust connections, thermal conditions, and mechanical movement can affect the finished assembly.

For industrial and heavy-duty applications, experience with equipment integration can be particularly valuable because the fabrication must often accommodate real-world constraints rather than standardized dimensions.

The evaluation should ultimately focus on whether the fabricator can translate engineering requirements into a controlled, manufacturable assembly. This approach supports a more meaningful procurement decision than treating DPF housing fabrication as a commodity metalworking service.

Custom DPF Housing Fabrication by The Sigma Source

The Sigma Source can support custom fabrication projects that require engineered metal components rather than standardized off-the-shelf parts. Its fabrication capabilities include stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, sheet metal, laser cutting, plasma cutting, welding, forming, machining, and related manufacturing processes.

For a DPF housing project, the appropriate scope can begin with the available drawings, equipment information, dimensions, material requirements, mounting geometry, exhaust interfaces, and operating conditions. From that information, the fabrication requirements can be defined around the actual equipment rather than relying on a generic enclosure configuration.

CAD and 3D modeling can be useful where custom geometry, installation constraints, or multiple interfaces need to be coordinated before production. Fabrication processes can then be selected according to the specified material, geometry, tolerances, and production requirements.

The same engineering discipline is important when a DPF housing is part of a larger industrial installation. Supporting brackets, structural interfaces, exhaust components, or vibration-related requirements may need to be coordinated with the surrounding equipment and project engineering.

At the same time, fabrication should be clearly distinguished from emissions certification. Producing a housing to engineering specifications does not by itself certify the emissions performance of a complete DPF or aftertreatment system. Where EPA, CARB, manufacturer, or jurisdiction-specific requirements apply, the responsible parties should establish those requirements before fabrication.

For OEMs, contractors, engineers, and procurement professionals seeking custom DPF housing fabrication, a useful starting package includes the DPF and equipment dimensions, connection details, material requirements, operating conditions, mounting information, drawings or CAD files, quantity, and applicable specifications. This gives the fabrication team the information needed to determine an appropriate manufacturing approach and project scope.

Conclusion: Engineering Considerations for DPF Housing Fabrication

A DPF housing is a fabricated mechanical component that must work within a larger diesel exhaust and equipment system. Successful DPF housing fabrication therefore depends on more than producing a correctly shaped enclosure. The housing must be developed around the DPF dimensions, exhaust interfaces, mounting arrangement, operating temperature, thermal cycling, vibration environment, service requirements, and available installation space.

Material selection should follow the actual operating environment. Stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, and specialized alloys each have different characteristics, and the appropriate choice depends on temperature, corrosion exposure, mechanical requirements, fabrication methods, and the location of the component. Welding, forming, machining, cutting, and assembly processes should likewise be selected around the required geometry and tolerances.

For retrofit projects, accurate field measurements and existing equipment information can be as important as the fabrication process itself. For OEM applications, CAD development, prototype validation, repeatable manufacturing, and quality control can help establish a consistent production assembly. In either case, clearly defining the fabrication scope helps prevent dimensional conflicts and misunderstandings about responsibility for emissions-system compliance.

U.S. projects may also involve EPA or CARB requirements, while IBC, CBC, ASCE 7, AWS, ASTM, SAE, ASME, or facility-specific requirements may apply depending on the equipment and installation. These standards should be addressed according to their actual relevance rather than presented as universal requirements for every DPF housing.

The Sigma Source's custom metal fabrication capabilities provide a foundation for projects requiring application-specific stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, sheet metal, cutting, forming, machining, and welded assemblies. For a project involving a custom DPF housing, the most productive starting point is a defined technical package containing equipment information, dimensions, connection geometry, material requirements, operating conditions, mounting details, drawings or CAD data, and applicable specifications.

Frequently Asked Questions About DPF Housing Fabrication

What is DPF housing fabrication?

DPF housing fabrication is the manufacture of the metal enclosure or canister used to package and mechanically support a diesel particulate filter within an exhaust or aftertreatment system. Depending on the application, the fabricated assembly can include inlet and outlet connections, mounting brackets, reinforcement, sensor ports, inspection access, heat shields, and other application-specific features. The housing should be distinguished from the DPF filter substrate itself, which performs the particulate-filtration function.

What materials are commonly used for DPF housings?

Common materials can include stainless steel and carbon steel, while aluminum and specialized alloys may be considered for particular components or applications. Material selection should be based on actual operating temperature, corrosion exposure, mechanical loading, weight requirements, fabrication characteristics, and project specifications. A material that is suitable for a lower-temperature support component may not be suitable for a portion of the housing exposed directly to high exhaust temperatures.

Can a DPF housing be custom fabricated to fit existing equipment?

Yes. Custom fabrication can accommodate equipment-specific dimensions, mounting points, exhaust connections, restricted installation envelopes, and retrofit requirements. Existing drawings, accurate field measurements, photographs, CAD models, and equipment documentation can help establish the required geometry. The fabricator should also understand which interfaces must remain unchanged and which components can be modified as part of the retrofit.

Can DPF mounting brackets and supports be fabricated?

Yes. A custom DPF assembly can incorporate mounting brackets, support plates, reinforcement structures, hangers, and other fabricated interfaces when those features are defined by the project. The support arrangement should be coordinated with the equipment structure and operating environment so that the housing is adequately supported without unnecessarily transferring loads into exhaust connections or other components.

What information is needed to fabricate a custom DPF housing?

A useful project package includes DPF dimensions, engine and equipment information, inlet and outlet dimensions, connection types, mounting locations, operating-temperature information, available installation space, material requirements, sensor locations, exhaust routing, environmental exposure, finish requirements, production quantity, and applicable specifications. CAD drawings or approved reference models can further reduce ambiguity when complex interfaces are involved.

Is stainless steel suitable for DPF housing fabrication?

Stainless steel can be appropriate for many exhaust-related applications, but the specific grade should be selected according to the actual conditions. Temperature, corrosion exposure, mechanical requirements, fabrication methods, and environmental conditions all influence the selection. Grades such as 304 or 316 may be appropriate in some applications, but neither should be treated as a universal solution without reviewing the project requirements.

Does DPF housing fabrication require EPA or CARB certification?

Not automatically. A fabricator producing a metal housing is not necessarily certifying the emissions performance of the complete DPF or aftertreatment system. EPA and CARB requirements can become relevant when the fabricated component forms part of a regulated emissions-control system. The responsible equipment manufacturer, emissions specialist, engineer, or other qualified party should establish the applicable requirements for the specific engine, equipment, configuration, and jurisdiction.

Can DPF housings be fabricated for diesel generators?

Yes. Generator applications can require custom housings because of enclosure dimensions, engine configuration, exhaust routing, mounting locations, thermal conditions, and surrounding equipment. A fabricated housing can be developed around the available installation envelope and the specified exhaust interfaces. The design should account for operating conditions and should be coordinated with the generator and aftertreatment system requirements.

Can DPF housings be fabricated for retrofit applications?

Yes. Retrofit projects can involve replacement housings, modified exhaust connections, new mounting arrangements, or housings designed around equipment where the original component is no longer available. Accurate dimensional information is particularly important for retrofit work because the new assembly must interface with existing components. Applicable emissions and equipment requirements should also be reviewed before modifications are made.

What fabrication processes are used to manufacture DPF housings?

Depending on the design, fabrication can involve CAD development, laser cutting, plasma cutting, sheet metal forming, rolling, machining, TIG or MIG welding, assembly, dimensional inspection, and application-specific finishing. The appropriate process depends on material, thickness, geometry, tolerances, production volume, and required documentation. Complex assemblies may use several processes within one manufacturing workflow.

Can DPF housing fabrication include sensor ports and inspection access?

Yes. Sensor ports, inspection openings, service access, and other features can be incorporated into a custom housing when their location and dimensions are established by the equipment or engineering requirements. Temperature sensors, differential-pressure connections, and maintenance access should be positioned according to the requirements of the applicable system rather than added without reference to the overall aftertreatment configuration.

How do I request a custom DPF housing fabrication project?

Begin with the available technical information: DPF and engine details, equipment application, dimensions, exhaust inlet and outlet geometry, mounting locations, operating conditions, material requirements, drawings or CAD files, required quantity, and applicable project specifications. The more clearly the interfaces and operating environment are defined, the easier it is to establish the fabrication scope, manufacturing processes, inspection requirements, and appropriate material selection. For a custom project, The Sigma Source can evaluate the available fabrication information and determine which of its metal fabrication and CAD capabilities are relevant to the required assembly.

items.content_html:
Custom isolator design is an engineering process used when a standard vibration mount cannot adequately address the load, frequency, geometry, environmental, or performance requirements of a specific installation. Rather than selecting an isolator solely from a catalog load rating, engineers evaluate the complete relationship between equipment mass, center of gravity, mounting points, operating speed, excitation frequency, stiffness, static deflection, damping, displacement, and the supporting structure.

This distinction becomes important for industrial machinery, HVAC equipment, generators, compressors, pumps, marine engines, precision equipment, and other systems where transmitted vibration can affect equipment reliability, structural performance, occupant comfort, acoustic conditions, or process quality. A custom vibration isolation system may also be necessary when equipment has an unusual bolt pattern, limited mounting envelope, uneven loading, elevated temperature exposure, corrosive conditions, or demanding alignment requirements.

Effective custom isolator design also requires coordination beyond the isolator itself. The mounting plate, equipment base, inertia base, support frame, structural attachment, anchor, and building structure form a connected equipment-to-structure interface. For installations in seismic regions, operational vibration isolation must also be coordinated with applicable seismic restraint and anchorage requirements.

The engineering workflow therefore moves from equipment characterization to vibration analysis, isolator selection, structural coordination, detailed CAD development, fabrication, installation, and verification. Depending on the application, spring, wire rope, rubber/metal, elastomeric, acoustic, floor, marine, or captive configurations may be appropriate. No single technology is universally suitable.

For U.S. projects, applicable project specifications, equipment requirements, structural criteria, and jurisdictional codes must be considered together. ASCE 7, IBC, and CBC can become particularly relevant when isolation systems interface with seismic restraint, equipment anchorage, or supporting structures. For applicable California healthcare facilities, HCAI requirements may also affect the engineering and documentation process.

What Is Custom Isolator Design?

Custom isolator design develops a vibration isolation solution around the actual behavior and requirements of the equipment rather than adapting the application to a standard mount. A standard isolator may provide an appropriate load range but still have unsuitable stiffness, natural frequency, displacement capacity, dimensions, attachment geometry, or environmental resistance.

How Custom Isolator Design Differs From Standard Mount Selection

Standard mount selection generally begins with equipment weight and an available product rating. Custom engineering goes further by determining how the equipment interacts dynamically with its supports. A 10,000-pound machine, for example, does not necessarily require four isolators rated for 2,500 pounds each. Its center of gravity, support-point locations, operating forces, base stiffness, and uneven reactions can produce substantially different loads at individual mounting points.

Performance requirements can also drive customization. If equipment operates at a particular rotational speed, the isolator system must be evaluated relative to that excitation frequency. Static load capacity alone does not establish whether the system will provide effective vibration isolation.

What Information Is Required for Isolator Engineering?

A useful design package may include equipment weight, dimensions, center of gravity, mounting-point coordinates, bolt pattern, operating speed, excitation frequencies, dynamic forces, allowable displacement, equipment-base details, support conditions, temperature range, chemical exposure, and manufacturer requirements. Existing installations may additionally require field measurements.

This information allows engineers to establish the required stiffness and isolation characteristics while determining whether a spring, wire rope, elastomeric, rubber/metal, acoustic, floor, or captive configuration is appropriate. The result is an isolation assembly developed around a defined engineering problem rather than a generic product category.

When Does Equipment Require a Custom Vibration Isolator?

Custom vibration isolators become particularly valuable when the equipment or installation falls outside the assumptions built into standard isolation products. The trigger may be performance, geometry, environment, structural limitations, or a combination of several factors.

Nonstandard Loads and Mounting Geometry

Large machinery can have concentrated loads, elevated centers of gravity, unusual mounting elevations, or asymmetric support reactions. Equipment may also have mounting holes that do not align with commercially available isolation mounts. A custom mounting plate, bracket, isolation rail, or support frame can solve these interface issues without compromising the equipment arrangement.

Performance-Specific Requirements

Custom engineering is also appropriate when a project has a defined vibration criterion. Natural frequency, static deflection, stiffness, damping, transmissibility, and allowable displacement should be evaluated together. An isolator that supports the equipment safely may still transmit unacceptable vibration if its dynamic characteristics are poorly matched to the operating conditions.

Retrofit and Replacement Applications

Retrofit projects create additional constraints because the existing foundation, structural members, housekeeping pad, equipment base, piping, ductwork, and access paths are already established. Replacing an existing mount with a standard component may not provide sufficient clearance or align with existing anchors.

A custom solution can account for existing dimensions while preserving equipment alignment and maintaining necessary clearances. Field verification is particularly important where original drawings are incomplete or modifications have accumulated over the life of a facility.

How Are Custom Isolators Engineered for Equipment Loads?

Load characterization is one of the fundamental steps in custom isolator engineering. The design must account for how equipment weight and operational forces are transferred through individual isolators and ultimately into the supporting structure.

Load Distribution and Center of Gravity

Individual isolator reactions depend on the equipment mass, center of gravity, support locations, and geometry. If the center of gravity is offset from the mounting plane, vertical reactions may not be equal. Large equipment can therefore require different isolator capacities or stiffness characteristics at different locations.

Engineers also consider whether the equipment base itself is sufficiently rigid. A flexible equipment frame can redistribute loads in ways that differ from a rigid-body assumption, making the interface between the equipment and isolation system an important part of the analysis.

Static and Dynamic Loading

Static loading represents the supported weight, while dynamic loading results from operating forces. Rotating machinery can generate periodic forces associated with operating speed, while reciprocating machinery may produce more complex force spectra. Impact or transient loads can also affect isolator selection.

Equipment Alignment and Support Geometry

Alignment is especially important for motors, pumps, compressors, generators, engines, and coupled machinery. The isolator arrangement must support the equipment without creating unacceptable tilt or differential movement. Mounting-plane elevations, lateral stability, bolt locations, and allowable displacement all influence the final configuration.

A technically sound design therefore considers the equipment, isolation mounts, mounting hardware, support structure, and attachment points as one mechanical system.

How Do Natural Frequency, Stiffness, and Damping Affect Isolation?

Vibration isolation is fundamentally frequency-dependent. The performance of an isolation system depends on the relationship between the excitation frequency and the system's natural frequency, as well as the stiffness and damping characteristics of the isolators.

Natural Frequency and Static Deflection

For a simplified spring-supported system, natural frequency is related to stiffness and supported mass. Greater static deflection in a spring system generally corresponds to lower vertical natural frequency. This is one reason static deflection is an important design parameter for spring isolators.

However, static deflection should not be treated as a complete measure of performance. Actual systems may involve multiple degrees of freedom, equipment-base flexibility, damping, horizontal stiffness, nonlinear behavior, and dynamic loading.

Frequency Ratio and Transmissibility

The frequency ratio compares excitation frequency with isolation-system natural frequency. Isolation generally becomes effective when the excitation frequency is sufficiently above the system's natural frequency. Near resonance, however, vibration response can increase substantially.

Consequently, custom isolator design should evaluate operating speed and relevant excitation frequencies before specifying stiffness. A mount that appears appropriate based only on load capacity may have unsuitable dynamic behavior.

Damping and Resonance Control

Damping influences the amplitude of response around resonance and affects how the system responds to transient excitation. Too little damping can result in pronounced resonance behavior, while additional damping can alter the system's transmissibility characteristics. The appropriate damping level depends on the application and performance objective.

For this reason, engineers should evaluate stiffness, damping, frequency, displacement, and load together instead of optimizing one parameter in isolation.

What Types of Custom Isolators Can Be Designed?

Different isolation technologies provide different combinations of stiffness, damping, displacement capability, durability, and environmental resistance. Selection should follow the application rather than a predetermined preference for one isolator type.

Custom Spring Isolators

Steel spring isolators can provide relatively low vertical natural frequencies and substantial static deflection for heavy mechanical equipment. They are frequently considered for HVAC equipment, pumps, fans, chillers, generators, and other machinery where low-frequency isolation is important.

Custom spring isolator design can address load ranges, spring geometry, mounting dimensions, lateral stability, vertical travel, and restrained or captive configurations. Where seismic requirements apply, restraint must be engineered so that required earthquake resistance does not unintentionally create an unwanted operational vibration path.

Custom Wire Rope Isolators

Wire rope isolators use formed wire-rope elements to provide multidirectional compliance. Their compact geometry, durability, and ability to accommodate vibration and shock make them useful in industrial, marine, transportation, and specialized equipment applications.

Geometry, wire diameter, strand construction, mounting arrangement, displacement requirements, and environmental exposure all influence performance.

Custom Rubber and Elastomeric Isolators

Rubber/metal mounts and elastomeric isolators can provide combined support and damping in compact assemblies. Material selection may depend on stiffness requirements, temperature, oils, chemicals, moisture, ozone, and other environmental conditions.

Acoustic, Floor, and Suspended Isolators

Acoustic hangers, floor vibration isolators, suspended isolation systems, and related configurations can address vibration transmission through building systems. HVAC applications may require coordination between equipment isolation, flexible duct and piping connections, structural supports, and ceiling or floor assemblies.

How Is Custom Isolator Design Applied to HVAC and Industrial Machinery?

HVAC and industrial applications frequently require isolation because operating machinery can transmit structure-borne vibration through building supports and connected services. The appropriate isolation strategy depends on equipment type, operating characteristics, support geometry, and project performance requirements.

HVAC Equipment

Air handling units, fans, pumps, chillers, cooling towers, rooftop units, and other mechanical equipment can produce operational vibration that travels through housekeeping pads, structural framing, piping, ductwork, and equipment connections.

Custom isolator engineering may be required when equipment dimensions, weight distribution, rooftop conditions, or mounting details do not align with standard products. Flexible connections should also be coordinated so that connected piping or ductwork does not create unintended rigid vibration paths.

Rotating and Reciprocating Machinery

Motors, compressors, generators, engines, and industrial machinery often require analysis of operating speed and excitation frequency. Rotating imbalance, reciprocating forces, gear-mesh frequencies, and other periodic sources may contribute to the vibration spectrum.

The isolator system must provide adequate support while allowing controlled movement. For high-cycle applications, fatigue and long-term durability can become important design considerations.

Precision and Vibration-Sensitive Equipment

Laboratories, semiconductor facilities, aerospace environments, precision manufacturing spaces, and sensitive measurement installations may have stricter vibration criteria than conventional building applications. In these environments, small structural or mechanical disturbances can affect process accuracy or equipment performance.

Custom isolation may therefore involve carefully controlled stiffness, damping, mounting geometry, and support conditions rather than simply increasing the size or capacity of a standard mount.

How Are Marine and Industrial Environments Considered in Custom Isolator Engineering?

Environmental conditions can change the suitability and service life of an isolation system. A design intended for an indoor mechanical room may not be appropriate for marine propulsion, industrial processing, or high-temperature exhaust-adjacent equipment.

Marine Engine Mounts

Marine engines and auxiliary equipment can experience continuous vibration, shock, limited installation space, alignment requirements, moisture, and saltwater exposure. Marine engine mounts must therefore be evaluated for the combined mechanical and environmental demands of the installation.

Wire rope and specialized elastomeric systems may be considered where multidirectional compliance, compactness, or shock response is important. The equipment-to-hull or equipment-to-frame interface must also be evaluated.

Temperature and Chemical Exposure

Elastomer properties can change with temperature and chemical exposure. Oils, solvents, fuels, cleaning agents, moisture, and saltwater can affect material performance depending on the specific compound.

Metal components may require stainless steel, suitable alloy steel, galvanized surfaces, protective coatings, or other corrosion-control measures. Material selection should be based on actual exposure conditions rather than assuming that one material is appropriate for every environment.

Fatigue and Cyclic Loading

Springs, wire rope assemblies, welded brackets, fasteners, and elastomeric elements may experience repeated operational loading. High-cycle machinery can therefore require attention to fatigue, stress concentration, manufacturing quality, and service conditions.

How Does Custom Isolator Design Coordinate With Seismic Restraint?

Vibration isolation and seismic restraint address different engineering objectives. Vibration isolation is intended to reduce the transmission of operational vibration, while seismic restraint limits earthquake-induced movement and transfers applicable forces into the supporting structure.

Vibration Isolation vs. Seismic Restraint

An isolated piece of equipment needs to remain isolated during normal operation while also having an appropriate seismic restraint strategy where required. A rigid restraint installed incorrectly can bypass the intended isolation path and create vibration transmission.

Conversely, an isolation system with excessive freedom of movement may not satisfy seismic displacement or restraint requirements. The solution must therefore be coordinated rather than treating vibration and seismic design as unrelated disciplines.

Captive and Restrained Isolation Systems

Captive spring isolators, restrained isolators, and other restraint configurations can limit excessive movement while permitting the intended operational isolation behavior. Selection depends on required displacement, seismic demand, equipment geometry, and structural attachment conditions.

Structural Attachments and Load Paths

The isolator is only one element in the load path. Forces may pass through a mounting plate, support frame, inertia base, connection, anchor bolt or concrete anchor, and structural member before reaching the building structure.

For applicable seismic projects, ASCE 7 and adopted building-code provisions such as the IBC or CBC may influence equipment anchorage and nonstructural component requirements. The structural capacity of the attachment and supporting member must be considered rather than assuming that an isolator's rating establishes the capacity of the complete assembly.

What Materials Are Used for Custom Isolator Design?

Material selection affects strength, stiffness, durability, corrosion resistance, fatigue performance, and manufacturability. Custom assemblies may combine several materials rather than relying on a single material throughout.

Metals and Structural Components

Carbon steel and structural steel are commonly used for mounting plates, brackets, support frames, inertia bases, and fabricated interfaces. Stainless steel may be appropriate for corrosive or marine environments, while high-strength or alloy steels can be considered where specific mechanical properties are required.

Aluminum and sheet metal may be useful when weight, corrosion resistance, or fabrication geometry makes them appropriate. Material thickness, weldability, connection design, and expected loads should be established during engineering.

Elastomers and Rubber Compounds

Neoprene and other synthetic or natural rubber compounds can provide different stiffness and damping characteristics. The appropriate compound depends on temperature, chemical exposure, environmental conditions, and required mechanical performance.

Coatings and Corrosion Protection

Galvanizing, zinc-based coatings, powder coating, and other protective treatments can extend the service life of metal components in suitable environments. Coating selection should account for operating temperature, exposure, fabrication sequence, and compatibility with the base material.

How Does BIM 3D CAD Support Custom Isolator Engineering?

BIM and 3D CAD can turn a custom isolation concept into a coordinated physical interface. This becomes particularly valuable when isolators must fit within crowded mechanical rooms, rooftop equipment zones, industrial machinery areas, or retrofit installations.

Equipment and Structural Coordination

A coordinated model can show equipment bases, isolation mounts, mounting frames, structural steel, piping, ductwork, conduit, cable trays, and access zones together. This helps engineers determine whether the proposed isolation geometry can actually be installed.

Clash Detection and Installation Geometry

Potential conflicts between isolators and structural members, piping, ductwork, housekeeping pads, ceilings, or access requirements can be identified before fabrication. This is particularly useful where displacement clearances are required.

Fabrication Documentation

Once the geometry is established, CAD data can support mounting plates, brackets, custom equipment frames, isolation rails, and custom strut channels. The same coordinated information can guide laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, machining, and assembly.

This engineering-to-fabrication connection reduces the risk of producing a component that technically meets a calculation but cannot be installed in the actual project geometry.

How Are Custom Isolators Manufactured and Verified?

Custom isolator manufacturing should follow the engineering requirements established during design. Fabrication is not a substitute for engineering; it is the physical realization of an engineered configuration.

Engineering-to-Fabrication Workflow

A typical process begins with equipment data and performance requirements, followed by load analysis, isolation-system selection, detailed geometry, material selection, connection development, and drawing review. Fabrication can then proceed using appropriate cutting, forming, welding, machining, coating, and assembly processes.

For a custom steel interface, for example, laser or plasma cutting may produce mounting plates and brackets, forming may establish required bends, and welding or machining may complete the assembly. Surface treatment can follow when corrosion protection is specified.

Dimensional and Load Considerations

Mounting-hole locations, isolator spacing, spring or wire-rope geometry, elastomer dimensions, support elevations, and assembly tolerances should be controlled according to the design. Incorrect dimensions can change load distribution or interfere with equipment alignment.

Installation and Field Verification

Installation should verify orientation, leveling, load distribution, fastener installation, clearances, restraint configuration, and contact conditions. Retrofit projects may require field verification before final fabrication because existing conditions can differ from drawings.

When Should a Project Use Custom Isolator Manufacturing?

Custom manufacturing becomes appropriate when the isolation system must interface with equipment or structures that cannot be accommodated by standard components. The need may originate with the isolator itself or with the surrounding mounting assembly.

Custom Equipment Interfaces

Unique mounting plates, brackets, inertia bases, support frames, and isolation rails can provide the required interface between equipment and isolators. This can be particularly useful for machinery with unusual footprints or bolt patterns.

Integrated Isolation and Support Assemblies

Some projects require an engineered assembly in which isolation mounts, steel frames, brackets, structural attachments, and equipment supports are developed together. This approach can simplify coordination because the physical interface is designed as a complete system.

Retrofit and Replacement Projects

Existing foundations and structural members can impose constraints that make conventional products difficult to install. Custom fabrication can accommodate existing elevations, anchor locations, limited access, and equipment dimensions without unnecessarily reconstructing surrounding systems.

The key is to maintain a clear relationship between engineering calculations, CAD geometry, fabrication drawings, and field installation requirements.

How The Sigma Source Supports Custom Isolator Design Projects

Custom isolator projects often cross several engineering and manufacturing disciplines. The Sigma Source can support this workflow by connecting vibration isolation engineering with structural coordination, seismic requirements, BIM/CAD development, and custom fabrication.

Vibration Isolation Engineering

The engineering process begins with equipment loads, operating conditions, excitation characteristics, mounting geometry, environmental exposure, and project performance requirements. This establishes the basis for selecting or developing an appropriate isolation configuration.

Depending on the application, spring isolators, wire rope isolators, rubber/metal isolators, acoustic hangers, floor vibration isolators, marine engine mounts, or captive vibration isolators may be considered.

Structural and Seismic Coordination

When an isolation system interfaces with a structural or seismic requirement, seismic calculations, structural engineering, equipment anchorage, seismic bracing, and structural attachments can be coordinated with the isolation design. The objective is to maintain a complete and traceable load path without confusing operational vibration control with earthquake restraint.

For applicable California healthcare projects, HCAI requirements and project-specific documentation should be incorporated into the engineering process where required.

BIM and Custom Fabrication

BIM 3D CAD modeling can establish equipment and support geometry, identify clashes, and produce coordinated fabrication information. Where standard components are insufficient, custom equipment mounting frames, structural supports, custom strut channels, mounting plates, and brackets can be fabricated from carbon steel, stainless steel, structural steel, aluminum, or other specified materials.

The fabrication workflow can incorporate laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, machining, galvanizing, and powder coating as appropriate.

A practical project workflow is:

Equipment characterization → load analysis → vibration requirements → custom isolator engineering → structural and seismic coordination → BIM/CAD → attachment and support design → fabrication where required → installation → field verification

Frequently Asked Questions About Custom Isolator Design

What is custom isolator design?

Custom isolator design is the engineering development of a vibration isolation system around the specific characteristics of equipment and its installation. It considers equipment mass, center of gravity, mounting points, operating frequency, dynamic loading, stiffness, static deflection, damping, displacement, environmental exposure, and support geometry. The objective is not simply to find a mount capable of carrying the equipment weight, but to establish an isolation system with characteristics appropriate to the application.

When is a custom vibration isolator better suited than a standard mount?

A custom vibration isolator may be appropriate when standard products cannot satisfy required load distribution, natural frequency, static deflection, displacement, geometry, environmental resistance, or attachment conditions. Retrofit equipment, unusual bolt patterns, asymmetric loads, marine machinery, high-cycle industrial equipment, and vibration-sensitive installations can all create conditions where a standard catalog configuration requires modification or replacement with an engineered solution.

What information is needed to design a custom vibration isolator?

Engineers generally need equipment weight, dimensions, center of gravity, mounting-point locations, bolt pattern, operating speed, excitation frequencies, dynamic loads when available, allowable displacement, equipment-base information, support conditions, and environmental requirements. Manufacturer data is particularly useful for rotating and reciprocating machinery. For existing installations, field measurements and photographs can help verify actual conditions.

How are natural frequency and static deflection used in isolator design?

For a simplified spring system, natural frequency is related to supported mass and stiffness, while static deflection is related to the spring's supported load and stiffness. Greater spring deflection generally corresponds to lower natural frequency. However, static deflection alone does not establish total isolation performance. Engineers should also evaluate excitation frequency, damping, horizontal behavior, displacement, equipment-base flexibility, and the specific performance criteria applicable to the project.

What is the difference between spring, wire rope, and rubber isolators?

Spring isolators commonly provide substantial vertical compliance and can be effective for heavy equipment requiring low natural frequencies. Wire rope isolators provide multidirectional compliance and can be useful where compactness, durability, vibration, or shock response is important. Rubber and elastomeric mounts provide different combinations of stiffness and damping in compact configurations. The correct choice depends on load, frequency, displacement, environment, geometry, durability, and project requirements rather than a universal preference for one technology.

Can custom isolators be designed for HVAC and industrial machinery?

Yes. Custom isolation systems can be engineered for air handling units, fans, pumps, chillers, cooling towers, generators, compressors, motors, industrial engines, and other machinery. The design should account for equipment weight, operating speed, dynamic forces, support geometry, connected piping or ductwork, structural conditions, and applicable vibration criteria. HVAC applications may also require coordination with flexible connections and seismic restraint.

Can a custom isolator also accommodate seismic restraint requirements?

A custom isolation assembly can be coordinated with seismic restraint requirements when the project requires both functions, but vibration isolation and seismic restraint remain distinct engineering objectives. The restraint configuration must limit applicable earthquake movement without unnecessarily bypassing the isolation system during normal operation. The complete seismic load path may include the isolator assembly, restraint, connectors, anchors, support frame, and building structure.

What materials are commonly used for custom vibration isolators?

Custom assemblies may use carbon steel, structural steel, stainless steel, high-strength steel, alloy steel, aluminum, spring steel, wire rope, and elastomeric compounds. Rubber and neoprene may be used for specific isolation elements, while stainless steel or protective coatings can be selected for corrosive environments. Galvanizing and powder coating are possible protective treatments when compatible with project conditions.

Can custom isolators be fabricated for marine or corrosive environments?

Yes, but the environmental conditions must be part of the engineering requirements. Marine installations can involve saltwater, humidity, shock, vibration, restricted space, and equipment alignment requirements. Industrial environments may introduce oils, chemicals, elevated temperatures, or repeated cycling. Material, elastomer, fastener, coating, and fabrication choices should therefore be based on the actual service environment and expected exposure.

How does BIM 3D CAD support custom isolator design and fabrication?

BIM and 3D CAD allow equipment, isolators, support frames, structural members, piping, ductwork, conduit, and access requirements to be coordinated spatially. This can identify clashes before fabrication and help establish accurate mounting geometry. Coordinated CAD information can then support fabrication drawings and manufacturing processes such as laser cutting, plasma cutting, forming, welding, and machining.

When does custom isolator manufacturing require custom mounting frames or support structures?

Custom mounting frames may be necessary when equipment has an unusual footprint, nonstandard bolt pattern, concentrated loading, unusual elevation, limited installation space, or structural attachment constraints. An engineered frame can distribute equipment reactions among isolators and create a controlled interface with the building structure. The frame itself should be evaluated for strength, stiffness, connections, anchorage, and compatibility with equipment alignment.

Can The Sigma Source engineer and fabricate custom isolation systems?

The Sigma Source's capabilities span vibration isolation products, engineering, BIM 3D CAD modeling, structural and seismic coordination, and custom metal fabrication. Depending on project requirements, this can connect equipment characterization and isolation engineering with spring, wire rope, rubber/metal, acoustic, floor, marine, or captive isolation configurations, followed by custom mounting plates, support frames, brackets, or related fabricated components where required.
